claims.claim: A Christian can fight as a soldier in a just war with a clear conscience.

stances.summary: A Christian may not be a soldier at all, not even a private who never has to sacrifice or carry out executions. When Christ disarmed Peter, He took the sword from every soldier.
stances.quote: still the Lord afterward, in disarming Peter, unbelted every soldier. No dress is lawful among us, if assigned to any unlawful action.
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, 1885
stances.original: Quomodo autem bellabit, immo quomodo etiam in pace militabit sine gladio, quem dominus abstulit? Nam etsi adierant milites ad Iohannem et formam obseruationis acceperant, si etiam centurio crediderat, omnem postea militem dominus in Petro exarmando discinxit. Nullus habitus licitus est apud nos illicito actui adscriptus.
stances.context: The chapter opens by asking whether a believer may enlist and whether soldiers may be admitted to the faith, 'even the rank and file... to whom there is no necessity for taking part in sacrifices or capital punishments', and answers no. The sentence just before the quote reads: 'But how will a Christian man war, nay, how will he serve even in peace, without a sword, which the Lord has taken away?' Date of On Idolatry is debated (roughly 198-211). He argues the same at length in The Crown (De corona) 11, written about 211 in his Montanist period: 'Shall it be held lawful to make an occupation of the sword, when the Lord proclaims that he who uses the sword shall perish by the sword? And shall the son of peace take part in the battle when it does not become him even to sue at law?' There he allows that men converted while already soldiers are a different case, but says they must quit ('which has been the course with many'), resort to quibbling, or face martyrdom. His objections mix killing with idolatry (oath, standards, sacrifices). Earlier, in the Apology (197), he boasted that Christians 'sail with you, and fight with you' (42) and fill 'the very camp' (37): a description of what Christians were doing, not a ruling; Apology 37 also says Christians count it 'better to be slain than to slay'. In later life he joined the Montanists (heterodox); never venerated as a saint. Do NOT copy from newadvent.org's page for On Idolatry: its text filter prints the word 'unbelted' as 'unbe**d'.

stances.summary: Christians do not fight for the emperor even when he orders it. They help him more by prayer, keeping their hands clean of blood like priests.
stances.quote: And none fight better for the king than we do. We do not indeed fight under him, although he require it; but we fight on his behalf, forming a special army--an army of piety--by offering our prayers to God.
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: Written about 248 in answer to the pagan Celsus, who urged Christians to fight for the emperor. In the same chapter Origen concedes that others may fight 'in a righteous cause' for 'the king who reigns righteously', and says Christians pray for them while keeping 'their hands pure', as pagan priests are exempted from service. So he does not call all war unjust; he says Christians do not kill. See also 5.33 ('we no longer take up sword against nation, nor do we learn war any more, having become children of peace, for the sake of Jesus') and 3.7 (Christ 'nowhere teaches that it is right for His own disciples to offer violence to any one, however wicked'). The CCEL plain-text file is used because newadvent.org's page breaks the dashes of this sentence with links. Origen was later judged heterodox on other points (Origenism condemned at Constantinople in 553).

stances.summary: God's command not to kill has no exceptions. A just man may not serve as a soldier, and may not even bring a capital charge, because killing itself is forbidden.
stances.quote: Thus it will be neither lawful for a just man to engage in warfare, since his warfare is justice itself, nor to accuse any one of a capital charge, because it makes no difference whether you put a man to death by word, or rather by the sword, since it is the act of putting to death itself which is prohibited.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7, 1886
stances.original: Ita neque militare iusto licebit, cuius militia est ipsa iustitia; neque vero accusare quemquam crimine capitali: quia nihil distat utrumne ferro, an verbo potius occidas; quoniam occisio ipsa prohibetur.
stances.context: Written about 303-311, during the Great Persecution. The next sentence: 'with regard to this precept of God, there ought to be no exception at all; but that it is always unlawful to put to death a man, whom God willed to be a sacred animal.' The passage sits in a chapter against gladiatorial shows and the exposure of infants. Later Lactantius became tutor to Constantine's son Crispus, and in On the Deaths of the Persecutors (about 315) he told approvingly of Constantine's victory under the sign of Christ; the surviving text of this passage was not changed. The Latin was read on a secondary site (lexchristianorum.blogspot.com), not a critical edition.

stances.summary: A soldier who wants to be baptized must refuse to kill, even under orders. A believer who wants to enlist is turned away, because he has despised God.
stances.quote: If a catechumen or a believer seeks to become a soldier, they must be rejected, for they have despised God.
stances.translation: Burton Scott Easton, The Apostolic Tradition of Hippolytus, Cambridge 1934; public domain in the US (copyright not renewed; Project Gutenberg #61614)
stances.context: Rules for examining the trades of people who ask to become catechumens. Two lines earlier: 'A soldier of the civil authority must be taught not to kill men and to refuse to do so if he is commanded, and to refuse to take an oath; if he is unwilling to comply, he must be rejected' (Easton's footnote markers removed). The next rule: 'A military commander or civic magistrate that wears the purple must resign or be rejected.' So a serving soldier could stay if he would not kill; enlisting was forbidden. ATTRIBUTION IS DISPUTED: the church order survives only in later Coptic, Arabic, Ethiopic and partial Latin versions, no Greek original, and many scholars now doubt it is by Hippolytus or from a single date (traditionally about 215). A softer 4th-century reworking, Apostolic Constitutions 8.32, only asks that a soldier 'do no injustice' and be 'content with his allotted wages'. Hippolytus himself was a rival bishop to Callistus of Rome, later reconciled and venerated as a martyr. If the quiz names Hippolytus, say 'the church rules long attributed to Hippolytus'.

stances.summary: War is murder on a grand scale that the world calls virtue. A hand that has held the Eucharist should not be stained with the sword and blood.
stances.quote: The whole world is wet with mutual blood; and murder, which in the case of an individual is admitted to be a crime, is called a virtue when it is committed wholesale.
stances.translation: Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.context: Written about 246, soon after his conversion, as a survey of the cruelty of the pagan world (robbers, pirates, wars, the arena, the courts). It condemns war as the world wages it but does not rule on Christian soldiers, hence strength 1. In On the Good of Patience 14 (256) he lists manslaughter among mortal crimes and says that 'after the Eucharist carried in it' the hand must not be 'spotted with the sword and blood'. The CCEL plain-text file is used because newadvent.org's page puts a link tag against the comma after 'murder'.

stances.summary: Now that I serve Christ I will not fight. I will stand unarmed in front of the battle line with only the sign of the cross, to show it is faith and not fear.
stances.quote: Hitherto I have served you as a soldier: allow me now to become a soldier to God: let the man who is to serve you receive your donative: I am the soldier of Christ: it is not lawful for me to fight.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 11, 1894
stances.original: Hactenus, inquit ad Caesarem, militavi tibi: patere ut nunc militem Deo: donativum tuum pugnaturus accipiat, Christi ego miles sum: pugnare mihi non licet.
stances.work: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St. Martin
stances.context: Martin's words as recorded by his disciple Sulpicius Severus, who knew him and wrote about 396; Martin left no writings. Said to Julian Caesar at a donative before a battle against invading barbarians near Worms (356). Julian accused him of cowardice; Martin offered to stand unarmed before the line 'protected by the sign of the cross, and not by shield or helmet'. The enemy sued for peace the next day. Context from chapters 2-3: a veteran's son, he was enrolled in the guard against his will and stayed 'nearly two years after he had received baptism', 'although but in name', at the request of his tribune. Historians question Sulpicius's timeline. Note the surrounding narrative in this translation uses lower case for pronouns of God ('his own soldier'); the quote itself has none.

stances.summary: Leave the army and serve Christ. A soldier with a sword serves death: he cannot win without shedding blood, and it makes no difference that the emperor is now a Christian.
stances.quote: He who soldiers with the sword is death's servant. Whenever he sheds his own blood or another's, from this he reaps the fruit of his pay. […] A soldier in war, though he fights not so much for himself as for another, must either meet his own death if beaten or, if he wins, become the cause of a death. He cannot win unless he has first shed blood.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin of W. Hartel, CSEL 29 (Vienna, 1894)
stances.original: et qui militat gladio mortis est minister, qui quando suum aut alienum sanguinem fundit, hinc recipit fructum stipendiorum; aut enim exitu mortis tenebitur reus aut crimine, quia necesse est, ut miles in bello, in quo tamen non tam pro se quam pro alio dimicat, aut suam mortem uictus inueniat aut mortis causam uictor adquirat, quia uictor esse non poterit, si effusor sanguinis ante non fuerit.
stances.context: Written about 400 to Crispinianus, a young Christian soldier in Gaul. The Latin was read in the scanned OCR of Hartel's edition (line numbers and hyphenation removed, OCR 'tarn' read as 'tam'). The same section goes on: 'You cannot serve two masters... Christ and Caesar', and in Hartel's text adds 'even though Caesar himself now seeks to be Christ's servant' (Hartel's emendation 'nunc'; the manuscripts read 'non'). The appeal is ascetic as much as moral: he also warns against wealth and marriage and urges a monastic life; a second letter (25*) repeats the plea. Paulinus had himself been governor of Campania before renouncing the world. The only complete English (P. G. Walsh, Ancient Christian Writers 35-36, 1966-67) is under copyright, so this is my own close rendering. Walsh's introduction confirms the aim: 'to stress the incompatibility of serving Christ and Caesar'.

stances.summary: Isaiah's prophecy of swords beaten into ploughshares has come true. Christians who once killed each other now refuse to make war even on their enemies.
stances.quote: and we who formerly used to murder one another do not only now refrain from making war upon our enemies, but also, that we may not lie nor deceive our examiners, willingly die confessing Christ.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: About 155, quoting Isaiah 2:3-4 as fulfilled in the Church. Dialogue with Trypho 110 says the same: 'we who were filled with war, and mutual slaughter, and every wickedness, have each through the whole earth changed our warlike weapons'. He gives no ruling on soldiers; in the same chapter he holds up soldiers' loyalty to their military oath as a model for martyrs. Strength 1: a clear sentiment in passing.

stances.summary: The Gospel has turned the nations' swords into ploughshares. Christians no longer know how to fight; when struck, they turn the other cheek.
stances.quote: did form the swords and war-lances into ploughshares, and changed them into pruning-hooks for reaping the grain, [that is], into instruments used for peaceful purposes, and that they are now unaccustomed to fighting, but when smitten, offer also the other cheek
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: About 180. An argument that Isaiah 2 and Micah 4 were fulfilled by the apostles' preaching; the peaceful Christian nations prove it. He does not discuss Christian soldiers. Weigh against Against Heresies 5.24.2, where he defends the ruler's sword as appointed by God 'so that under the fear of human rule, men may not eat each other up like fishes', and says magistrates acting 'in a just and legitimate manner, shall not be called in question for their conduct'. So: against Christians fighting in spirit, not against the state's use of force. Thin evidence; do not make him a headline result on this claim.

stances.summary: Christ taught us not to repay evil with evil. We would rather shed our own blood than stain our hands and consciences with another's.
stances.quote: that it is better to suffer wrong than to inflict it, that we should rather shed our own blood than stain our hands and our conscience with that of another
stances.translation: Hamilton Bryce and Hugh Campbell, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 6, 1886
stances.context: About 300, by a recent convert rebutting the charge that Christians caused the empire's wars. A general statement of Christian non-retaliation, not a ruling on military service. Not in the results pool.

stances.summary: I am a Christian, so I cannot serve as a soldier or do what soldiers do. Other Christians in the army must answer for themselves.
stances.quote: they know what is good for them ; but I am a Christian, and cannot do what is wrong.
stances.translation: Arthur James Mason, The Historic Martyrs of the Primitive Church (Longmans, 1905), pp. 206-207; Mason renders the Acts inside his own narrative
stances.original: Ipsi sciunt quod ipsis expediat. Ego tamen Christianus sum, et non possum mala facere.
stances.context: A 21-year-old veteran's son, called up at Theveste in Numidia and beheaded for refusing. The proconsul Dion answered him: 'There are Christian soldiers in the sacred bodyguard of our lords Diocletian and Maximian, Constantius and Maximus : they serve.' The quote is his reply. Asked what wrong soldiers do, he said 'you know well enough what they do.' He also refused the lead seal worn round the neck as incompatible with 'the saving sign' of Christ, so idolatry and violence are both in view. The space before the semicolon is the scanned book's typography; copy it as is for the machine check. Latin checked in Mabillon's edition on la.wikisource.org (Passio sancti Maximiliani), long-s scanning gaps removed. The earliest recorded Christian conscientious objector. Not in the results pool.

stances.summary: A Christian serves Christ the eternal King, so he should not serve the emperor's army or the cares of the world. I throw down my belt and my arms.
stances.quote: For it was not right for a Christian, who serves the Lord Christ, to serve the cares of the world.
stances.translation: E. C. E. Owen, Some Authentic Acts of the Early Martyrs (Oxford, 1927), p. 123
stances.context: A centurion who had served as a Christian until the emperor's birthday feast at Tingis on 21 July 298, when, 'deeming those banquets to be heathen', he threw down his belt, vine-switch and arms, saying 'I serve Jesus Christ the Eternal King' and refusing sacrifice to 'gods of wood and stone'. His break was triggered by idolatry more than by killing, hence strength 1. The Acts survive in two recensions; Owen translates Knopf's text. Not in the results pool.

stances.summary: Killing is wrong in general, but in war it is lawful and even praiseworthy to destroy the enemy. The same act can be wrong in one setting and right in another.
stances.quote: For example, it is not right to kill, yet in war it is lawful and praiseworthy to destroy the enemy; accordingly not only are they who have distinguished themselves in the field held worthy of great honours, but monuments are put up proclaiming their achievements.
stances.translation: Archibald Robertson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: A letter to the monk Amun about whether involuntary bodily emissions make a monk unclean. War is used as an illustration that the same act can be lawful in one setting and not in another; the letter is not about war. Strength 1 for that reason, though the line is stated without hesitation. The letter was later counted among Athanasius's canonical letters in Eastern church law.

stances.summary: Killing in war is not murder, and a soldier can love God perfectly. But hands that have killed are not clean, so a soldier who has killed should stay away from communion for three years.
stances.quote: Homicide in war is not reckoned by our Fathers as homicide; I presume from their wish to make concession to men fighting on behalf of chastity and true religion. Perhaps, however, it is well to counsel that those whose hands are not clean only abstain from communion for three years.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 8, 1895
stances.context: Written in 374 to Amphilochius of Iconium; the canon entered Orthodox canon law. A deliberate middle view: war killing is excused, not murder, yet it leaves a stain that calls for penance ('perhaps... it is well to counsel', so advice rather than a fixed rule). He also praised a Christian soldier in Letter 106: 'I have learned to know one who proves that even in a soldier's life it is possible to preserve the perfection of love to God'. This is the best source for a quiz position of 'justified, but not with a clear conscience'.

stances.summary: Courage that defends the homeland from invaders in war is full of justice. Whoever can protect a neighbour from harm and does not is as guilty as the one who harms him.
stances.quote: For courage, which in war preserves one's country from the barbarians, or at home defends the weak, or comrades from robbers, is full of justice;
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 10, 1896
stances.original: Fortitudo quae vel in bello tuetur a barbaris patriam, vel domi defendit infirmos, vel a latronibus socios, plena iustitiae est.
stances.work: On the Duties of the Clergy (De officiis)
stances.context: Written about 388-391, modelled on Cicero. Book 1 sections 175-177 praise the wars of Joshua, Gideon, Samson and David ('David never waged war unless he was driven to it'), though he says arms are not the clergy's business. Book 1 section 179: 'He who does not keep harm off a friend, if he can, is as much in fault as he who causes it.' Important limit: in book 3 section 27 he says a Christian should not kill even an armed robber to save his own life, 'lest in defending his life he should stain his love toward his neighbour'. So he accepts war for others but not private self-defense. The Latin is as excerpted in Ivo of Chartres, Panormia 8.34, and Gratian's Decretum C.23 q.3 c.5, where this line became a pillar of medieval just-war law. The CCEL text is used because newadvent.org puts link tags against the commas.

stances.summary: A soldier can please God. Wage war only when you must, always aiming at peace, and show mercy to the defeated.
stances.quote: Do not think that it is impossible for any one to please God while engaged in active military service.
stances.translation: J. G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 1, 1886
stances.original: Noli existimare neminem Deo placere posse, qui armis bellicis ministrat.
stances.context: About 418, to Boniface, a Christian general in Africa who was thinking of becoming a monk. He cites David, the centurion of Matthew 8, Cornelius and John the Baptist's words to soldiers (Luke 3:14). Section 6: 'Peace should be the object of your desire; war should be waged only as a necessity' and 'Let necessity, therefore, and not your will, slay the enemy who fights against you.' The same case recurs in Letter 138.15 (412: 'if the Christian religion condemned wars of every kind', John would have told soldiers to 'cast away their arms'), Against Faustus 22.74-75 (about 400: 'The real evils in war are love of violence, revengeful cruelty...'), City of God 1.21 and 19.7 (the wise man wages just wars but will 'lament the necessity of just wars'). He does not allow private self-defense killing (Letter 47.5), only a soldier or official acting for others. His famous change of mind concerns using force against the Donatists, not soldiering. Latin checked in Gratian's Decretum C.23 q.1 c.3.

stances.summary: Soldiering is no obstacle to a holy life. Cornelius was a centurion and his army belt did not spoil his devotion, so a soldier has no excuse.
stances.quote: The excuse cannot be founded in reason. For Cornelius was a centurion, yet in no way did the soldier's belt impair his strict rule of life.
stances.translation: Talbot W. Chambers, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 12, 1889
stances.context: Preached at Antioch, rebuking men who plead military duties as their excuse for skipping church while finding time for the theatre. Elsewhere: 'these things I say, not blaming crafts, nor husbandry, nor military service, but ourselves' (Homily 61 on Matthew, section 3), and 'Wouldest thou see men saved in the rank of a soldier? there is Cornelius' (Homily 12 on Philippians). He treats soldiering as a lawful calling but does not discuss killing in war directly, hence strength 1. Caution: 'Christians above all men are not permitted forcibly to correct the failings of those who sin' (On the Priesthood 2.3) is about a pastor's discipline of sinners, not war.

stances.summary: There are two ways of Christian life. The perfect way gives up marriage, property and worldly affairs; the ordinary way may marry, govern and command soldiers fighting for a right cause.
stances.quote: And the other more humble, more human, permits men to join in pure nuptials and to produce children, to undertake government, to give orders to soldiers fighting for right; it allows them to have minds for farming, for trade, and the other more secular interests
stances.translation: W. J. Ferrar, The Proof of the Gospel, 1920
stances.work: The Proof of the Gospel (Demonstratio evangelica)
stances.context: Written about 314-318, just after the persecutions ended. The ordinary way is given 'a kind of secondary grade of piety'. So fighting for a right cause is allowed to ordinary Christians but is not part of the higher life. Eusebius later wrote the Life of Constantine and was suspected of Arian sympathies. Not in the results pool.

stances.summary: A Christian general's victories are God's gift. He wages war not from love of bloodshed but to widen a realm where God is worshipped and Christ is preached.
stances.quote: And report goes that it is not from a desire of shedding blood that you constantly court these wars, but for the sake of extending the republic in which we see that God is worshipped, to the end that the name of Christ may be spread abroad through subject nations by preaching of the faith.
stances.translation: James Barmby, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 12, 1895
stances.work: Register of Letters, to Gennadius, exarch of Africa
stances.context: Written in the first year of his papacy (590-591) to Gennadius, the imperial governor of Africa, who was waging frontier wars. The letter before it (1.74) opens: 'As the Lord has made your Excellency to shine with the light of victories in the military wars of this life'. Gregory never argues the point; he assumes a Christian general's wars can be holy. The CCEL text is used because newadvent.org puts a link tag against the comma after 'wars'.

stances.summary: Keep your trade when you come to faith, soldier included, but obey the Commander who orders what is right. Christians are trained for peace, not war.
stances.quote: Practise husbandry, we say, if you are a husbandman; but while you till your fields, know God. Sail the sea, you who are devoted to navigation, yet call the while on the heavenly Pilot. Has knowledge taken hold of you while engaged in military service? Listen to the commander, who orders what is right.
stances.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: About 195. Read with the farmer and sailor beside it, the line seems to let a converted soldier stay in service, with God as his real commander; but 'the commander' may mean God, and the line may only say that knowledge of God found him there. Elsewhere Clement says 'it is not in war, but in peace, that we are trained' (The Instructor 1.12) and 'The one instrument of peace, the Word alone by which we honour God, is what we employ' (The Instructor 2.4); in The Instructor 3.12 he repeats John the Baptist's rule that soldiers be 'content with their wages only'. No clear ruling on killing, hence mixed and strength 1.

stances.summary: A man can be holy in a soldier's uniform. But the better way is to leave the army and its money behind and follow Christ as a monk.
stances.quote: Who can fail to love a man who, while he wears the cloak and uniform of a soldier does the work of a prophet
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Date unknown. After the praise, Jerome urges the soldier Exuperantius to come to Bethlehem and become a monk, adding 'I have a notion that your object in remaining so long in the army is to fill that purse which the Lord has commanded you to empty.' The objection is ascetic (money and the world), not killing: soldiering is compatible with holiness, but leaving is better. The NPNF note says Exuperantius came but left again. Thin evidence on war itself.

splits_fathers: Real voices on both sides, divided mostly by era. Before Constantine (to about 313) every writer who addresses the question is against a Christian killing in war or enlisting: Tertullian, Origen, the Apostolic Tradition, Cyprian, Lactantius, Arnobius, with Justin and Irenaeus in passing; the martyrs Maximilian (295) and Marcellus (298) died for it. Yet Christians plainly served (Tertullian's own Apology 37 and 42; the proconsul's remark to Maximilian; Marcellus had served as a Christian centurion), and Clement seems to let a converted soldier stay. Many early objections mix killing with idolatry (oaths, standards, sacrifices). After 313 the bishops who write on it accept war in a right cause: Athanasius, Ambrose, Augustine, Chrysostom (as a lawful calling), Eusebius (for the 'secondary' life) and Gregory the Great. Two currents keep the older view alive: ascetics who urge soldiers to leave (Martin, Paulinus, Jerome more mildly), and Basil's canon, which excuses war killing yet asks three years away from communion. Clearest contrasts: Tertullian, Origen or Lactantius against Augustine or Ambrose; Martin against Augustine; Basil as the middle.
splits_people_today: Lopsided toward agree. Most Christians (Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches, which teach or accept just-war thinking) and most non-religious people would say a soldier in a just war does nothing wrong. A real but small minority disagrees: the historic peace churches (Mennonites, Quakers, Church of the Brethren), Christian pacifists across denominations, and principled pacifists outside the Church. The words 'with a clear conscience' pull in a third group: people who think killing in war can be justified yet still leaves a wound (today often called moral injury in veterans). That is almost exactly Basil's position, and it may split ordinary people more evenly than the bare question. Another split that reverses modern intuition: Ambrose and Augustine accept killing in war but forbid killing an attacker in private self-defense, while most people today find self-defense the easier case.

misattributions.line: Above all, Christians are not allowed to correct with violence the delinquencies of sins.
misattributions.attributed_to: Clement of Alexandria (for example on the English Wikipedia page 'Christianity and violence', and many anti-war quote lists)
misattributions.truth: The idea is John Chrysostom's, On the Priesthood 2.3 (NPNF1 vol. 9: 'For Christians above all men are not permitted forcibly to correct the failings of those who sin'). It is about a bishop's pastoral discipline of sinners (persuasion, not force), not about war or soldiering.

misattributions.line: Christ, in disarming Peter, disarmed every soldier.
misattributions.truth: A loose paraphrase of On Idolatry 19. Thelwall's translation reads 'unbelted every soldier' (Latin 'discinxit': took off the military belt). newadvent.org's copy prints the word as 'unbe**d' because of a text filter, so quote it from tertullian.org or CCEL.

misattributions.line: I am a soldier of Christ; I cannot fight.
misattributions.truth: Genuine in substance but not Martin's own writing: it is his reported speech in Sulpicius Severus, Life of St. Martin 4 (about 396). The scene is before a battle near Worms in front of Julian Caesar, not the cloak scene at Amiens it is sometimes attached to.

misattributions.line: A soldier must be taught not to kill; a believer who wants to become a soldier must be rejected, for he has despised God.
misattributions.truth: From the Apostolic Tradition, whose authorship by Hippolytus and single date (about 215) are disputed; it survives only in later translations. Cite it as 'attributed to Hippolytus'.

misattributions.line: Christians could not slay their enemies.
misattributions.attributed_to: Origen (quoted this way on Wikipedia as a statement on war)
misattributions.truth: Genuine words (Against Celsus 7.26) but about why Moses' civil laws (stoning, burning, killing enemies) could not be kept by Christians under Roman rule, not about military service. His direct statement on soldiering is Against Celsus 8.73.

misattributions.line: The letter of Marcus Aurelius to the Senate crediting Christian soldiers' prayers for the rain that saved his army (the 'Thundering Legion').
misattributions.attributed_to: Marcus Aurelius (printed after Justin's First Apology in ANF vol. 1)
misattributions.truth: A later Christian forgery; ANF vol. 1 itself notes 'Spurious, no doubt'. Its line that Christians began the battle 'not by preparing weapons, nor arms, nor bugles; for such preparation is hateful to them' circulates in quote lists as evidence of early Christian pacifism: it is not from any Father. Tertullian (Apology 5) does report the rain story as answered prayer of Christians 'fighting under him', so the story is early, but the letter is not genuine.

notes: 1) Pool gaps: in the time spent I found no statement on this question from Ignatius, Perpetua, Novatian, Antony, Ephrem, Hilary, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa, Macrina, Amma Syncletica, Moses the Black, Arsenius, Poemen, Evagrius, Pelagius, John Cassian, Benedict, Boethius, John Climacus or Isaac the Syrian. Do not assign them a side on this claim. (Ignatius, Cyprian, Paulinus, Benedict and the monks use soldier language constantly, but as a metaphor for the spiritual life; that is not evidence either way.) 2) Two reasons are tangled in the early objections: killing, and idolatry (the military oath, the standards, sacrifices, the emperor's cult). Origen, Lactantius, Cyprian and Paulinus object to killing itself; Marcellus mainly to idolatry; Tertullian and the Apostolic Tradition to both. After 313 the idolatry reason fell away. Canon 12 of Nicaea (325), which punishes those who took back the military belt after casting it off, concerns apostasy under Licinius, not killing. Canon 3 of the Council of Arles (314) excommunicates those who throw away their arms in peacetime; what it means is disputed, so it is not cited as evidence here. 3) Best pairs for the result reveal: Martin (unarmed before the battle line) against Augustine (Letter 189 to a general); Tertullian's 'unbelted every soldier' against Ambrose's 'full of justice'; Basil for the middle. 4) Several quotations come from CCEL plain-text volumes, archive.org scans and Project Gutenberg rather than newadvent.org because newadvent's links sit against punctuation or its filter alters words; the url given for each quote is the page it was checked against, and every non-own-rendering quote was matched by script against that page, with tags stripped both with and without spaces. 5) Capitals: none of the quotations contains a pronoun for God, but Ferrar, Mason and Owen print pronouns for God in lower case in the surrounding text, so check any longer excerpt. 6) Useful for cards: Maximilian was 21; Martin offered to face the enemy with only the sign of the cross; Basil's three years; Gregory's praise of a general's wars; Augustine's 'Let necessity, therefore, and not your will, slay the enemy'.
